#| label: setup

import pandas as pd

summary = pd.read_csv("data/ladder_summary.csv")
illus_blocks = pd.read_csv("data/illustration_blocks.csv", dtype={"tract_geoid": str})
illus_stores = pd.read_csv("data/illustration_stores.csv")
flags_v = pd.read_csv("data/validation_flags.csv")
shares_v = pd.read_csv("data/validation_shares.csv").set_index("distance_mi")
tract_v = pd.read_csv("data/validation_tracts.csv", dtype={"tract_geoid": str})
bounds = pd.read_csv("data/approximation_bounds.csv").set_index("step")

main = summary.loc[summary["variant"] == "1And10"].set_index("step")

def fmt(x):
    return f"{int(x):,}"

la = main["tracts_low_access"]
lila = main["tracts_lila"]
pop_la = main["pop_in_low_access_tracts"]

# Headline numbers (1-and-10-mile thresholds)
la_large, la_all = fmt(la[1]), fmt(la[5])
lila_large, lila_all = fmt(lila[1]), fmt(lila[5])
pop_large, pop_all = fmt(pop_la[1]), fmt(pop_la[5])
la_ratio = f"{la[1] / la[5]:.1f}"
lila_ratio = f"{lila[1] / lila[5]:.0f}"

# Tracts removed at each step, and each step's share of the total drop
la_drop = (-la.diff()).fillna(0)
lila_drop = (-lila.diff()).fillna(0)
dollar_la, dollar_lila = fmt(la_drop[2]), fmt(lila_drop[2])
dollar_la_share = f"{la_drop[2] / (la[1] - la[5]):.0%}"
dollar_lila_share = f"{lila_drop[2] / (lila[1] - lila[5]):.0%}"
conv_la = fmt(la_drop[4])

retail_pa = main["retailers_pa"]
retail_large, retail_all = fmt(retail_pa[1]), fmt(retail_pa[5])

# Validation against USDA's SRAM (step 5 = same store universe as SRAM)
v = flags_v.query("step == 5 and variant == '1And10'").set_index("measure")
kappa_la = f"{v.loc['Low access', 'kappa']:.2f}"
agree_la = f"{v.loc['Low access', 'agreement']:.1%}"
kappa_lila = f"{v.loc['Low income, low access', 'kappa']:.2f}"
s1 = shares_v.loc[1.0]
pop1_ours, pop1_sram = fmt(s1["pop_beyond_ours"]), fmt(s1["pop_beyond_sram"])
pop1_ratio = f"{s1['pop_ratio']:.0%}"
r1 = f"{s1['share_r']:.2f}"
within5_1 = f"{s1['within_5pp']:.0%}"
s10 = shares_v.loc[10.0]
pop10_ours, pop10_sram = fmt(s10["pop_beyond_ours"]), fmt(s10["pop_beyond_sram"])

# How many people the definition moves (large grocery -> every SNAP retailer)
combo_sum = pd.read_csv("data/combo_summary.csv")
impact_who = pd.read_csv("data/impact_who.csv")
impact_near = pd.read_csv("data/impact_nearest.csv")
beyond_large, beyond_all = main.loc[1, "pop_beyond_threshold"], main.loc[5, "pop_beyond_threshold"]
moved_people = fmt(beyond_large - beyond_all)
moved_share = f"{(beyond_large - beyond_all) / beyond_large:.0%}"
la_pop_drop = fmt(main.loc[1, "pop_in_low_access_tracts"] - main.loc[5, "pop_in_low_access_tracts"])
lila_pop_drop = fmt(main.loc[1, "pop_in_lila_tracts"] - main.loc[5, "pop_in_lila_tracts"])
near = impact_near.query("variant == '1And10' and people > 0").set_index("key")
near_conv = fmt(near.loc["convenience", "people"])
near_conv_share = f"{near.loc['convenience', 'people'] / near['people'].sum():.0%}"
near_dollar = fmt(near.loc["dollar", "people"])
who = impact_who.query("variant == '1And10'").set_index("group")
lose_snap_hh = fmt(who.loc["Lose low-income, low-access status", "Households receiving SNAP"])
lose_nov_hh = fmt(who.loc["Lose low-income, low-access status", "Households without a vehicle"])

# Illustration tract
METRES_PER_MILE = 1609.344
illus_tract = illus_blocks.loc[illus_blocks["in_tract"] == 1]
illus_tract_id = illus_tract["tract_geoid"].iloc[0]

illus_blocks_n = fmt(len(illus_tract))

illus_mi_all = f"{(illus_tract['dist_all_m'] * illus_tract['pop']).sum() / illus_tract['pop'].sum() / METRES_PER_MILE:.1f}"

# Block internal-point approximation

b5 = f"{bounds.loc[5, 'tracts_la_min']:,}–{bounds.loc[5, 'tracts_la_max']:,}"

## How the measure works

<!-- DRAFT (Sean): factual description of the method; edit into your voice. -->

The measure asks one question of every person in Pennsylvania: how far is the
nearest store that counts? It answers it census block by census block, then
rolls the answers up to census tracts, the unit USDA designates.

```{python}
#| label: method-figure
#| fig-cap: "Each dot is a census block's internal point, sized by population. Lines connect each block in the outlined tract to its nearest store."
#| fig-alt: "Two maps of the same neighborhood east of Pittsburgh. With only large grocery stores counted, lines from every block in the outlined tract run more than a mile to three stores outside it, and its dots are orange. With every SNAP retailer counted, the lines are short, run to stores inside the tract, and the dots are blue."
#| renderings: [light, dark]
import inspect
import json
import warnings

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

# Street basemap: OpenStreetMap's standard tiles (no API key), fetched once when
# the page renders and toned to grey so the data stays in front. Needs
# contextily; without it, or offline, the figure renders without a basemap.
try:
    import contextily as cx
except ImportError:
    cx = None
    warnings.warn("contextily not installed: method figure renders without a basemap")
TILES = "https://tile.openstreetmap.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.png"
# OpenStreetMap blocks tile requests that don't identify the app making them
# ("Access blocked" tiles), so name this site instead of contextily's random ID.
TILE_HEADERS = {"User-Agent": "sean-hudson-portfolio/1.0 (+https://sean-hudson-data.github.io)",
                "Referer": "https://sean-hudson-data.github.io/"}
if cx is not None:
    cx.tile.USER_AGENT = TILE_HEADERS["User-Agent"]


def tone(img, mode):
    """Greyscale the tiles: pale for light mode, inverted and dim for dark."""
    rgb = img[..., :3].astype(float)
    grey = rgb @ np.array([0.299, 0.587, 0.114])
    grey = 255 - (255 - grey) * 0.45 if mode == "light" else 18 + (255 - grey) * 0.3
    out = img.copy()
    out[..., :3] = np.clip(grey, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)[..., None]
    return out

with open("data/pa_tracts.geojson") as f:
    tract_geom = next(feat["geometry"] for feat in json.load(f)["features"]
                      if feat["properties"]["tract_geoid"] == illus_tract_id)
outline = (tract_geom["coordinates"] if tract_geom["type"] == "MultiPolygon"
           else [tract_geom["coordinates"]])
lat0 = illus_blocks["lat"].mean()
panels = [("large", "Large grocery retailers only", illus_stores["large"]),
          ("all", "Every SNAP retailer", illus_stores["large"] | True)]


def add_tiles(ax, mode, ink):
    """Draw map tiles under everything; leave the axes untouched if that fails.

    Tiles cover a padded window, because matplotlib widens one axis at draw time
    to keep the map's aspect ratio."""
    (w, e), (south, n) = ax.get_xlim(), ax.get_ylim()
    pad_x, pad_y = (e - w) * 0.4, (n - south) * 0.4
    try:
        extra = ({"headers": TILE_HEADERS}
                 if "headers" in inspect.signature(cx.bounds2img).parameters else {})
        img, ext = cx.bounds2img(w - pad_x, south - pad_y, e + pad_x, n + pad_y, zoom=14,
                                 source=TILES, ll=True, **extra)
        img, ext = cx.warp_tiles(tone(img, mode), ext, t_crs="EPSG:4326")
    except Exception as err:  # offline, or the tile server refused
        warnings.warn(f"basemap skipped: {err}")
        return
    ax.imshow(img, extent=ext, zorder=0, interpolation="bilinear")
    ax.set_xlim(w, e)
    ax.set_ylim(south, n)
    ax.text(0.995, 0.005, "© OpenStreetMap contributors", transform=ax.transAxes,
            ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=6, color=ink, alpha=0.8, zorder=5)


def share_label(share):
    pct = "over 99%" if 0.99 < share < 1 else f"{share:.0%}"
    return f"{pct} of the outlined tract's residents live more than a mile away"


def method_chart(mode):
    ink = "#343a40" if mode == "light" else "#e3e6ea"
    near = "#2a78d6" if mode == "light" else "#3987e5"
    far = "#eb6834" if mode == "light" else "#d95926"
    line = "#9aa0a6" if mode == "light" else "#6b7280"
    edge = "white" if mode == "light" else "#212529"

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 5.6), layout="constrained")
    fig.patch.set_alpha(0)
    for ax, (key, title, counts) in zip(axes, panels):
        ax.set_facecolor("none")
        ax.set_aspect(1 / np.cos(np.deg2rad(lat0)), adjustable="datalim")
        for _, r in illus_tract.iterrows():
            ax.plot([r["lon"], r[f"store_lon_{key}"]], [r["lat"], r[f"store_lat_{key}"]],
                    color=line, lw=0.6, alpha=0.7, zorder=1)
        beyond = illus_blocks[f"dist_{key}_m"] > METRES_PER_MILE
        ax.scatter(illus_blocks["lon"], illus_blocks["lat"],
                   s=np.sqrt(illus_blocks["pop"]) * 2.2, c=np.where(beyond, far, near),
                   alpha=0.8, linewidths=0, zorder=2)
        for poly in outline:
            x, y = zip(*poly[0])
            ax.plot(x, y, color=ink, lw=1.4, zorder=3)
        s = illus_stores.loc[counts]
        ax.scatter(s["lon"], s["lat"], marker="s", s=34, color=ink, edgecolors=edge,
                   linewidths=0.8, zorder=4)
        share = (illus_tract.loc[illus_tract[f"dist_{key}_m"] > METRES_PER_MILE, "pop"].sum()
                 / illus_tract["pop"].sum())
        ax.set_title(f"{title}\n{share_label(share)}", loc="left", color=ink, fontsize=10.5)
        ax.set_xlim(illus_blocks["lon"].min(), illus_blocks["lon"].max())
        ax.set_ylim(illus_blocks["lat"].min(), illus_blocks["lat"].max())
        ax.set_xticks([])
        ax.set_yticks([])
        for spine in ax.spines.values():
            spine.set_visible(False)
        # 1-mile scale bar
        dlon = METRES_PER_MILE / (111_320 * np.cos(np.deg2rad(lat0)))
        x0, y0 = illus_blocks["lon"].min() + 0.002, illus_blocks["lat"].min() + 0.002
        ax.plot([x0, x0 + dlon], [y0, y0], color=ink, lw=2, zorder=5)
        ax.text(x0 + dlon / 2, y0 + 0.0015, "1 mile", ha="center", color=ink, fontsize=9,
                zorder=5)
        if cx is not None:
            add_tiles(ax, mode, ink)
    handles = [
        Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", color=near, label="Block within 1 mile"),
        Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", color=far, label="Block more than 1 mile away"),
        Line2D([], [], marker="s", ls="", color=ink, label="Store that counts"),
        Line2D([], [], color=line, label="Line to nearest store"),
    ]
    fig.legend(handles=handles, loc="outside lower center", ncol=4, frameon=False,
               labelcolor=ink, fontsize=9)
    plt.show()


method_chart("light")
method_chart("dark")
```

<!-- TODO: one or two sentences on the figure. The outlined tract (Allegheny County,
tract `r py$illus_tract_id`, `r py$illus_pop` residents in `r py$illus_blocks_n`
blocks) is on average `r py$illus_mi_large` miles from a large grocery store and
`r py$illus_mi_all` miles from any SNAP retailer. Name the place if you like. -->

Step by step:

1. **Start with people, where they live.** The 2020 Census counts population
   for every census block, the smallest unit it publishes (336,985 blocks in
   Pennsylvania, many no bigger than a city block). Each block is represented by
   its internal point, a location the Census Bureau places inside the block.
2. **Find the nearest store.** For each block, the straight-line distance to the
   nearest store that counts, measured along the Earth's surface. The search
   covers every store in the country, so a block near a state line can find a
   store across it.
3. **Pick the threshold.** USDA uses different distances for urban and rural
   tracts: 1 mile in urban tracts and 10 miles in rural ones (with ½-mile and
   20-mile variants). The urban flag is USDA's own, so the threshold for every
   tract matches theirs.
4. **Count the people beyond it.** Everyone in a block whose internal point is
   farther than the threshold counts as beyond it. Summing those blocks gives
   the number of people beyond the threshold in each tract, and dividing by
   the tract's population gives the share.
5. **Apply USDA's rule.** A tract is *low access* if at least 500 people, or at
   least a third of its residents, are beyond the threshold. It is *low income,
   low access* (the usual "food desert") if it is also one of USDA's
   low-income tracts.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Two numbers that both get called "people in food deserts"

- **People beyond the threshold**: only the people who live farther than the
  threshold from a store. This is the number in step 4.
- **People in low-access tracts**: everyone living in a tract that meets the
  rule, including neighbors who live next to a store. Headlines like "X million
  Americans live in food deserts" use this one, because the designation belongs
  to the tract.

The second is always larger. This page says which one it means each time.
:::

## How USDA measures it

<!-- DRAFT (Sean): check against the ERS documentation linked below. -->

USDA's Food Access Research Atlas now comes in two versions, and both answer the
same question with a different picture of where people live.

- **The Large Retailer Access Map (LRAM)** is the original atlas. It spreads 2010
  Census population evenly across half-kilometer grid squares and measures from
  each square to the nearest supermarket, supercenter, or large grocery store,
  using a 2019 store list and 2010 tract boundaries.
- **The SNAP-authorized Retailer Access Map (SRAM)**, released in July 2026, draws
  a circle of each threshold distance around every SNAP-authorized store (as of
  June 2025) and counts the people outside every circle, using LandScan USA's
  roughly 90-meter population grid and 2020 tracts.

Both then apply the same low-access rule as step 5. A circle of a mile around
every store and the distance to the nearest store are two views of the same
thing: someone is outside every circle exactly when their nearest store is more
than a mile away. So the three approaches differ mainly in where they put people
and which stores they count.

| | This page | USDA LRAM (original atlas) | USDA SRAM |
|---|---|---|---|
| Where people are | 2020 census block internal points | 2010 Census, spread over 0.5 km grid squares | LandScan USA, ~90 m grid |
| Stores | SNAP Retailer Locator, August 2026; any combination of types | Large grocery retailers, 2019 list | All SNAP retailers except farmers markets, June 2025 |
| Distance | Straight line to the nearest store | From each grid square to the nearest store | Circles around each store; straight-line and driving versions |
| Tracts | 2020 | 2010 | 2020 |
| Can change which stores count? | Yes | No | No |

Holding everything but the store list fixed is the point: it lets the ladder
and map below isolate the definition, and "Does it reproduce USDA's numbers?"
checks the method against SRAM.

## Why the definition matters

- LRAM counts only large grocery retailers; SRAM counts every SNAP retailer,
  including dollar stores and chain pharmacies. Which is right is a judgment
  about what counts as food access, and the answer moves the map. -->

```{python}
#| label: ladder-chart
#| fig-cap: "Pennsylvania census tracts flagged under each definition (1 mile urban, 10 miles rural)"
#| fig-alt: "Two horizontal bar charts. Low-access tracts fall from 1,018 under large grocery retailers to 486 under all SNAP retailers, with the biggest drops at dollar stores and convenience stores. Low-income, low-access tracts fall from 220 to 36, mostly at the dollar store step."
#| renderings: [light, dark]
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

labels = main["label"].tolist()
panels = [("Low-access tracts", la), ("Low-income, low-access tracts", lila)]


def ladder_chart(mode):
    ink = "#343a40" if mode == "light" else "#e3e6ea"
    muted = "#5f6670" if mode == "light" else "#aab1ba"
    bar = "#2a78d6" if mode == "light" else "#3987e5"

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.6), sharey=True,
                             layout="constrained")
    fig.patch.set_alpha(0)
    for ax, (title, values) in zip(axes, panels):
        y = range(len(values))
        ax.barh(y, values.to_numpy(), color=bar, height=0.62)
        for yi, val in zip(y, values.to_numpy()):
            ax.text(val + values.max() * 0.02, yi, f"{val:,}", va="center",
                    color=ink, fontsize=10)
        ax.set_title(title, loc="left", color=ink, fontsize=11.5)
        ax.set_xlim(0, values.max() * 1.18)
        ax.set_facecolor("none")
        ax.tick_params(colors=muted, length=0)
        ax.set_xticks([])
        for side in ("top", "right", "bottom", "left"):
            ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
    axes[0].set_yticks(range(len(labels)), labels, color=ink, fontsize=10)
    axes[0].invert_yaxis()  # shared y: inverting once flips both panels
    plt.show()


ladder_chart("light")
ladder_chart("dark")
```

## Does the threshold change the story?

<!-- TODO: one sentence. The ordering of steps holds at every threshold; the
half-mile urban threshold flags more tracts under every definition. -->

```{python}
#| label: tbl-thresholds
#| tbl-cap: "Low-access tracts by definition and distance threshold"
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
names = {"1And10": "1 mi urban / 10 mi rural", "halfAnd10": "½ mi / 10 mi",
         "1And20": "1 mi / 20 mi"}
wide = (summary.assign(threshold=summary["variant"].map(names))
        .pivot(index="label", columns="threshold", values="tracts_low_access")
        .reindex(main["label"])[list(names.values())])
cols = list(names.values())
print("| Definition | " + " | ".join(cols) + " |")
print("|---|" + "---:|" * len(cols))
for label, r in wide.iterrows():
    print(f"| {label} | " + " | ".join(f"{int(x):,}" for x in r) + " |")
```

### Which stores put them within reach?

<!-- TODO takeaway. For the `r py$moved_people` people who move, this is the kind
of store that is now their nearest. Convenience stores are the nearest new store

This complements the ladder: the ladder credits dollar stores with the biggest

```{python}
#| label: nearest-chart
#| fig-cap: "People beyond the threshold with large grocery retailers only but within it with every SNAP retailer, by the type of store now nearest to them"
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bar chart. Convenience stores are the nearest new store for about 1.08 million people, dollar stores for about 262,000, chain pharmacies for about 117,000, and other and specialty stores for under 30,000 each."
#| renderings: [light, dark]
near_plot = near.sort_values("people")


def nearest_chart(mode):
    ink = "#343a40" if mode == "light" else "#e3e6ea"
    bar = "#2a78d6" if mode == "light" else "#3987e5"
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 2.8), layout="constrained")
    fig.patch.set_alpha(0)
    ax.set_facecolor("none")
    y = range(len(near_plot))
    ax.barh(y, near_plot["people"], color=bar, height=0.62)
    for yi, val in zip(y, near_plot["people"]):
        ax.text(val + near_plot["people"].max() * 0.015, yi, f"{val:,}", va="center",
                color=ink, fontsize=10)
    ax.set_yticks(list(y), near_plot["label"], color=ink, fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xlim(0, near_plot["people"].max() * 1.15)
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.tick_params(length=0)
    for side in ("top", "right", "bottom", "left"):
        ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
    plt.show()


nearest_chart("light")
nearest_chart("dark")
```

#| label: tbl-who

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## How sure are these counts?

- **Against USDA.** With every SNAP retailer, this method counts within 2% of
  USDA's own figure for people more than a mile from a store in urban tracts
  (see "Does it reproduce USDA's numbers?").
- **The block approximation.** Counting every ambiguous block as entirely inside
  or entirely beyond the threshold puts people beyond it at `r py$pb1` with large
  grocery retailers only and `r py$pb5` with every SNAP retailer. Even taking the
  lowest figure for the first and the highest for the second, the wider definition
  moves at least `r py$moved_min` people.
- **Other thresholds.** The same comparison at each threshold:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-impact-thresholds
#| tbl-cap: "People beyond the threshold, by threshold"
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
names = {"1And10": "1 mi urban / 10 mi rural", "halfAnd10": "½ mi / 10 mi",
         "1And20": "1 mi / 20 mi"}
print("| Threshold | Large grocery retailers only | Every SNAP retailer | Difference |")
print("|---|---:|---:|---:|")
for v, label in names.items():
    r = summary.loc[summary["variant"] == v].set_index("step")
    a, b = r.loc[1, "pop_beyond_threshold"], r.loc[5, "pop_beyond_threshold"]
    print(f"| {label} | {a:,} | {b:,} | −{a - b:,} |")
```

## Pick the stores that count

<!-- TODO takeaway: which places drop out first. Readers can check and uncheck store
types and see which tracts change. Suggest trying dollar stores alone, or
everything except convenience stores. -->

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
tracts = FileAttachment("data/tract_combos.csv").csv({typed: false})
shapes = FileAttachment("data/pa_tracts.geojson").json()
storeTypes = FileAttachment("data/store_types.csv").csv({typed: true})
comboSummary = FileAttachment("data/combo_summary.csv").csv({typed: true})

viewof picked = Inputs.checkbox(storeTypes, {
  label: "Stores that count",
  format: d => `${d.label} (${d.stores_pa.toLocaleString()} in PA)`,
  value: storeTypes.filter(d => d.key === "supermarket" || d.key === "grocery")
})

viewof threshold = Inputs.radio(
  new Map([["1 mile urban, 10 miles rural", "1And10"],
           ["½ mile urban, 10 miles rural", "halfAnd10"],
           ["1 mile urban, 20 miles rural", "1And20"]]),
  {label: "Distance threshold", value: "1And10"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Bit c of each tract's hex string = low access under store-type combination c,
// where bit g of c = store type g (see _analysis/01_store_types.py).
combo = picked.reduce((c, d) => c | (1 << d.bit), 0)
largeOnly = storeTypes.filter(d => d.key === "supermarket" || d.key === "grocery")
                      .reduce((c, d) => c | (1 << d.bit), 0)
allTypes = storeTypes.reduce((c, d) => c | (1 << d.bit), 0)
isLA = (t, c) => (parseInt(t[`la_${threshold}`][c >> 2], 16) >> (c & 3)) & 1

byTract = new Map(tracts.map(d => [d.tract_geoid, d]))
statusOf = id => {
  const t = byTract.get(id)
  if (!t) return "Not low access"
  if (isLA(t, combo)) return "Low access with these stores"
  if (isLA(t, largeOnly)) return "Low access with large grocery retailers only"
  return "Not low access"
}

tally = c => {
  const la = tracts.filter(t => isLA(t, c))
  return {n: la.length, lila: la.filter(t => t.low_income === "1").length,
          pop: d3.sum(la, t => +t.pop2020)}
}
now = tally(combo)
base = tally(largeOnly)
beyond = c => comboSummary.find(d => d.variant === threshold && d.combo === c)?.pop_beyond ?? 0
note = combo === largeOnly ? " This is FARA and LRAM's large-retailer definition."
     : combo === allTypes ? " This is SRAM's definition: every SNAP retailer except farmers markets."
     : ""

md`${picked.length === 0
  ? "**Pick at least one store type.**"
  : `**${now.n.toLocaleString()} low-access tracts** (${now.lila.toLocaleString()} also low income), home to ${now.pop.toLocaleString()} people. **${beyond(combo).toLocaleString()} people** live beyond the threshold.<br>With large grocery retailers only: ${base.n.toLocaleString()} tracts (${base.lila.toLocaleString()} low income) and ${beyond(largeOnly).toLocaleString()} people beyond the threshold.${note}`}`
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Leaflet on OpenStreetMap tiles (no API key), greyed with CSS to match the page theme
L = require("leaflet@1.9.4")
leafletCss = html`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/leaflet@1.9.4/dist/leaflet.css">
<style>
  .osm-tiles { filter: grayscale(1) brightness(1.04) contrast(0.85); }
  body.quarto-dark .osm-tiles { filter: grayscale(1) invert(1) brightness(0.8) contrast(0.85); }
</style>`

palette = ({
  "Low access with these stores": {fill: "#eb6834", opacity: 0.75},
  "Low access with large grocery retailers only": {fill: "#6da7ec", opacity: 0.6},
  "Not low access": {fill: "#000000", opacity: 0}
})

legend = html`<div style="display:flex; gap:1.25rem; flex-wrap:wrap; font-size:0.85rem; margin:0.25rem 0 0.5rem;">
  ${Object.entries(palette).slice(0, 2).map(([label, s]) => html`<span style="display:inline-flex; align-items:center; gap:0.4rem;">
    <span style="width:14px; height:14px; border-radius:3px; background:${s.fill}; opacity:${s.opacity + 0.2};"></span>${label}</span>`)}
</div>`

mapEl = {
  leafletCss;
  const el = html`<div style="height:560px; border-radius:6px;"></div>`
  // Resolves with the tract layer once Leaflet has built it, so the restyle
  // cell below waits for it instead of running too early on first load.
  let ready
  el._layer = new Promise(resolve => { ready = resolve })
  yield el

  const map = L.map(el, {preferCanvas: true, scrollWheelZoom: false, zoomSnap: 0.25})
  L.tileLayer("https://tile.openstreetmap.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.png", {
    attribution: '&copy; <a href="https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright">OpenStreetMap</a> contributors',
    maxZoom: 19, className: "osm-tiles"
  }).addTo(map)

  const layer = L.geoJSON(shapes, {style: {weight: 0.4, color: "#6c757d", opacity: 0.35,
                                            fillOpacity: 0}}).addTo(map)
  map.fitBounds(layer.getBounds())
  ready(layer)
  invalidation.then(() => map.remove())
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Restyle and retitle the tracts whenever the store types or threshold change
restyle = {
  const layer = await mapEl._layer
  layer.eachLayer(l => {
    const id = l.feature.properties.tract_geoid
    const status = statusOf(id)
    const s = palette[status]
    l.setStyle({fillColor: s.fill, fillOpacity: s.opacity})
    const t = byTract.get(id) ?? {}
    l.unbindTooltip().bindTooltip(
      `<strong>${t.county ?? ""}, tract ${id.slice(5)}</strong><br>` +
      `Population: ${(+t.pop2020 || 0).toLocaleString()}<br>${status}`,
      {sticky: true})
  })
}
```

## Does it reproduce USDA's numbers?

<!-- TODO takeaway, one sentence: with the same stores as USDA's SRAM, the measure
matches USDA's published flags and counts closely, so differences across the
ladder come from the definition, not the method.

Why compare with SRAM and not the original FARA (now LRAM): LRAM still uses a
2019 store list and 2010 tract boundaries, so a gap against it would mix the
definition with old data. SRAM is USDA's current product, uses the same store
universe as step 5, and publishes both its flags and the number of people
beyond each distance for every tract. -->

**Tract designations.** With every SNAP retailer counted, this method and USDA
agree on `r py$agree_la` of Pennsylvania tracts' low-access status (Cohen's kappa
`r py$kappa_la`; LILA kappa `r py$kappa_lila`).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-validation
#| tbl-cap: "Agreement with USDA's published SRAM flags, Pennsylvania tracts (all SNAP retailers)"
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
names = {"1And10": "1 mi / 10 mi", "halfAnd10": "½ mi / 10 mi", "1And20": "1 mi / 20 mi"}
t = flags_v.query("step == 5").copy()
print("| Threshold | Measure | Tracts flagged (this method) | Tracts flagged (USDA) | Agreement | Kappa |")
print("|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|")
for _, r in t.iterrows():
    print(f"| {names[r.variant]} | {r.measure} | {r.ours_flagged:,} | {r.reference_flagged:,} "
          f"| {r.agreement:.1%} | {r.kappa:.2f} |")
```

**People beyond the threshold.** USDA also publishes, for every tract, how many
people live beyond each distance. In urban tracts this method counts
`r py$pop1_ours` people more than a mile from a SNAP retailer; USDA counts
`r py$pop1_sram` (`r py$pop1_ratio`). Tract by tract, the shares correlate at
`r py$r1`, and `r py$within5_1` of urban tracts are within 5 percentage points of
USDA's figure.

```{python}
#| label: validation-chart
#| fig-cap: "Share of each urban tract's residents more than 1 mile from a SNAP retailer: this method vs. USDA"
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of 2,494 urban Pennsylvania tracts. Points cluster tightly along the diagonal line where this method's share equals USDA's published share."
#| renderings: [light, dark]
urban_v = tract_v.loc[tract_v["urban"] == 1].dropna(subset=["ours_share_1", "sram_share_1"])


def validation_chart(mode):
    ink = "#343a40" if mode == "light" else "#e3e6ea"
    muted = "#5f6670" if mode == "light" else "#aab1ba"
    dot = "#2a78d6" if mode == "light" else "#3987e5"
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 5), layout="constrained")
    fig.patch.set_alpha(0)
    ax.set_facecolor("none")
    ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color=muted, linewidth=1, linestyle="--")
    ax.scatter(urban_v["sram_share_1"], urban_v["ours_share_1"], s=8,
               alpha=0.35 if mode == "light" else 0.55, color=dot, linewidths=0)
    ax.set_xlim(0, 1); ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
    ax.set_xlabel("USDA SRAM", color=muted)
    ax.set_ylabel("This method", color=muted)
    for axis in (ax.xaxis, ax.yaxis):
        axis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda x, _: f"{x:.0%}"))
    ax.tick_params(colors=muted, length=0)
    for side in ("top", "right"):
        ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
    for side in ("bottom", "left"):
        ax.spines[side].set_color(muted)
    plt.show()


validation_chart("light")
validation_chart("dark")
```

<!-- TODO: one sentence on rural tracts. With every SNAP retailer counted, almost
no one in Pennsylvania is 10 miles from a store (`r py$pop10_ours` people here vs.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## How much does the block approximation matter?

Everyone in a block gets the distance from the block's internal point. That's
exact for small city blocks and rough for large rural ones. To bound it, a block
counts as *ambiguous* when the threshold falls within its effective radius (the
radius of a circle with the block's land area), so part of it could sit on
either side.

`r py$amb1` of Pennsylvanians live in ambiguous blocks under the large-grocery
definition (`r py$amb5` with every SNAP retailer). Counting every ambiguous block
as entirely inside, then entirely beyond, the threshold puts low-access tracts at
`r py$b1` under the large-grocery definition and `r py$b5` with every SNAP
retailer. These are worst cases, since a real block is rarely all on one
side. Even at the extremes the ranges don't overlap, so the gap between the two
definitions is larger than anything the approximation could produce.

<!-- TODO (optional): the close match with USDA's SRAM above suggests the
approximation isn't biased in practice; USDA's own method approximates too. -->
:::

## Data, definitions, and validation

<!-- TODO: short list.
- Population: 2020 census blocks (TIGER/Line 2025), 336,985 PA blocks, each at its
  internal point.
- Retailers: USDA SNAP Retailer Locator, August 2026, searched nationally so border
  blocks can find stores in neighboring states.
- Low access: FARA's rule (at least 500 people or a third of the tract beyond the
  threshold), with USDA's own urban and low-income tract flags from SRAM.
- Validation: see "Does it reproduce USDA's numbers?" above. -->

The distance pipeline is [OS-FARA](TODO-link), an open-source replication of
USDA's Food Access Research Atlas. The ladder and map data are built by
[`projects/food-store-definitions/_analysis`](https://github.com/sean-hudson-data/sean-hudson-data.github.io/tree/main/projects/food-store-definitions/_analysis).

```{python}
#| label: combo-code
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
# One nearest-store search per store type (D: blocks x types, in metres).
# The nearest store in any combination of types is the closest of its types,
# so 7 searches cover all 127 combinations.
def combo_distance(c):
    cols = [g for g in range(len(TYPES)) if c >> g & 1]
    return D[:, cols].min(axis=1)
```
